title: Tech mascots: where the penguin, the Octocat and the gopher came from
description: Linux has a penguin, GitHub has a cat with octopus arms, Go has a gopher, and Firefox is named after an animal that isn't in its logo. Each Question asks where a mascot came from, what it was first called, or why the joke stuck. The Explanations also cover licensing, because whoever owns a mascot decides who may draw it. For anyone who has seen these characters on stickers and wondered about them.

questions.title: Linus Torvalds says a penguin once bit him. Where did it happen?
questions.description: He tells the story as the reason he became fond of penguins, before Linux had any mascot at all.

options.text: At the National Zoo & Aquarium in Canberra, Australia, where a little penguin nibbled him
At Helsinki Zoo, near the university where he wrote the first Linux kernel
On a beach on Phillip Island, where he tried to photograph wild penguins
At a research station in Antarctica, during a trip sponsored by a Linux company

questions.explanation:
Around 1993, Torvalds visited Australia to talk about Linux to the Australian Unix Users Group. At the zoo in Canberra, a little penguin nibbled him. Australians call the species the fairy penguin, and he later joked that the "ferocious fairy penguin" should be kept locked up.

Phillip Island is a reasonable guess. It is famous for its wild little penguins, and some retellings move the story there. Torvalds himself wrote in *Linux Journal* that it happened at the Canberra zoo.

The bite alone didn't make Tux the mascot. In May 1996, when people asked why Linux should have a penguin, he answered: "Linus likes penguins. That's it." The neater versions of the story came later.

questions.title: In May 1996, Linus Torvalds told the kernel mailing list what the Linux penguin should look like. What did he ask for?
questions.description: He was replying to a prototype logo that showed a penguin holding up the globe.

options.text: A slightly overweight, contented penguin sitting down, too stuffed with herring to stand up
A strong penguin holding up the world like Atlas, to show that Linux could carry serious workloads
A fierce penguin chasing the Windows logo, to show Linux was the challenger
A plain geometric penguin shape, simple enough to print in one colour on a floppy disk label

questions.explanation:
Torvalds rejected the globe prototype because the penguin didn't look strong enough to hold up the world. It looked about to be squashed, which is a poor image for a logo.

He asked people to think "cuddly", "cute" and "contented". For a penguin, he explained, contented means stuffed with herring: it sits down because it has eaten too much to stand, and smiles as if it has just burped. He also said he didn't want a "macho penguin".

A few days later he explained why he preferred a character to an abstract mark like the Windows logo. You can redraw a character doing something new, such as a penguin typing on a word processor, and people still recognise it. You can't do that with an abstract logo, which is why there are so many versions of Tux.
questions.references: [Linus Torvalds, "Re: Linux Logo prototype", linux-kernel, 9 May 1996 (archived by Steve Baker)](https://web.archive.org/web/2015/http://www.sjbaker.org/wiki/index.php?title=The_History_of_Tux_the_Linux_Penguin)

questions.title: Larry Ewing drew the penguin that became Tux. Which program did he use?

options.text: GIMP 0.54, the first public release of the free image editor
Adobe Photoshop 3.0, the standard tool for digital artists in 1996
Xfig, the vector drawing program that shipped with most Unix systems
Microsoft Paint, as a joke about Linux's rival

questions.explanation:
Ewing painted Tux in 1996 in GIMP 0.54, the first public release of the GNU Image Manipulation Program. A free-software mascot drawn with a free-software tool suited Linux well. Ewing also wrote up how he made it, as a guide to drawing in GIMP.

He released the image with one condition: you may use and modify it if you credit him and The GIMP "if someone asks". That is why the caption below names both.

Tux never won a logo contest. There were three, and Tux won none of them. Officially, Tux is the Linux *brand character* rather than its logo.

images.alt: The original Tux: a plump black-and-white penguin with a yellow beak and yellow feet, sitting down with a contented look.
images.caption: Larry Ewing's original 1996 Tux, placed on a white background. By Larry Ewing (lewing@isc.tamu.edu) and The GIMP, used under his use-with-credit permission, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tux.png).

questions.title: The first suggestion to call the penguin "Tux" explained the name as an acronym. The T stood for Torvalds. What did UX stand for?
questions.explanation:
On 10 June 1996, the day after Linux 2.0 came out, someone on the kernel mailing list proposed a contest to name the penguin. James Hughes replied with "(T)orvalds (U)ni(X) --> TUX!"

The acronym is a stretch, since the U and the X both come from one word. The name stuck for another reason: a penguin's black-and-white feathers look like a tuxedo, and "tux" is short for tuxedo.
questions.references: [James Hughes, "Re: Let's name the penguin!", linux-kernel, 10 June 1996 (archived by Steve Baker)](https://web.archive.org/web/2015/http://www.sjbaker.org/wiki/index.php?title=The_History_of_Tux_the_Linux_Penguin), [Wikipedia: Tux (mascot)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tux_%28mascot%29)

questions.title: Before GitHub renamed it, what was the Octocat called?

options.text: Octopuss
Mona
Inkitty
Gitcat

questions.explanation:
British illustrator Simon Oxley drew a character with a cat's head and octopus arms and sold it as stock clip art on iStock, under the name "Octopuss". GitHub's founders bought it for the site's error pages and renamed it the Octocat.

Mona is a real name too, but it came later. The daughter of a GitHub developer wrote a story about a cat called Monalisa who swallowed some coral and grew octopus legs. When GitHub wrote down the character's personality, it adopted the name Mona Lisa, or Mona for short.

That character guide has a rule you may not have noticed: the Octocat never speaks. Cameron McEfee, who wrote the guide, had watched talking mascots such as Clippy become annoying. The Octocat shows how it feels through its face and what it does.
questions.references: [Cameron McEfee: The Octocat](https://cameronmcefee.com/work/the-octocat/), [Wikipedia: GitHub, Mascot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GitHub#Mascot). Related Quiz: *The internet runs on cats*.

questions.title: Why did a half-cat, half-octopus fit GitHub so well?

options.text: Git has an "octopus merge", which combines three or more branches in one commit
Git's short commit hashes are eight characters long by default, one for each arm
GitHub was founded by eight people, one for each arm
Git stores file permissions as octal numbers

questions.explanation:
An ordinary merge commit has two parents. An octopus merge has more. If you name several branches in one command, Git uses the octopus strategy and records a single commit with one parent per branch:

```bash
git merge feature-a feature-b feature-c
```

The octopus strategy refuses any merge that needs manual conflict resolution. It is for bundling branches that don't conflict.

The other options are wrong. Git's short hashes are at least 7 characters by default and grow when needed to stay unique. GitHub had four founders. Git does record file modes such as `100644` in octal, but the mascot has nothing to do with them. And the Octocat has five arms, not eight.

questions.title: Simon Oxley, who drew the Octopuss, sold another stock illustration that became a famous tech logo. Which one?

options.text: The original Twitter bird
The Android robot
The Firefox fox
The Chrome offline dinosaur

questions.explanation:
Twitter's first bird logo was a cheap stock image by Oxley, bought from iStock. The Android robot, the Firefox fox and the Chrome dinosaur were all drawn for Google or Mozilla.

The licence explains why the two purchases ended differently. A standard stock licence lets many customers use the same image, so it doesn't allow a buyer to use it as a logo or trademark. GitHub wanted the Octopuss as its logo, so it negotiated with Oxley for exclusive rights, renamed the character and registered the Octocat as a trademark. Twitter had its bird redrawn instead, and later versions were new designs that Twitter owned.

questions.title: "Firefox" is a common name for which animal?

options.text: The red panda
The red fox
The fennec fox
The Arctic fox

questions.explanation:
Mozilla said the browser's name came from a nickname for the red panda. The logo still shows a fox wrapped around a globe. Jon Hicks, who drew the first logo in 2004, said a red panda "didn't really conjure up the right imagery", and few people knew the animal anyway.

The fennec fox is a fair guess, because Mozilla did use it: "Fennec" was the code name for the old mobile version of Firefox.

questions.title: Which names did the browser use before it became Mozilla Firefox in February 2004?

options.text: Phoenix
Mozilla Firebird
Mozilla Thunderbird
Camino

questions.explanation:
The browser started in 2002 as **Phoenix**, the bird that rises from the ashes, a nod to Netscape's defeat by Internet Explorer. Phoenix Technologies, a maker of PC BIOS software, claimed the trademark, so in 2003 the browser became **Firebird**.

That name clashed with the Firebird database, an open source project that complained loudly. Mozilla first promised to always write "Mozilla Firebird" to avoid confusion. After more pressure, it switched to Firefox on 9 February 2004.

The other two names are real but belong to other products. Thunderbird is Mozilla's email client, a sibling of the browser. Camino was a separate Mac browser built on Mozilla's engine.

questions.title: What was the Chrome offline dinosaur game's code name during development?

options.text: Project Bolan
Project Jurassic
Project Meteor
Project Sue

questions.explanation:
Sebastien Gabriel, Alan Bettes and Edward Jung of the Chrome UX team built the game in 2014. They called it Project Bolan, after Marc Bolan, the singer of T. Rex, so the code name is a dinosaur pun. Gabriel called the character the "Lonely T-Rex".

The game's world does have a meteor. If a network administrator disables the game, the error page shows a meteor heading for the dinosaur.

questions.title: Which statements about the Chrome offline dinosaur are true?

options.text: The dinosaur is a joke that having no internet connection is like living in prehistoric times
You can play it while online by typing `chrome://dino` in the address bar
Flying pterosaurs were added as obstacles in a later update
It appears when Google's servers are down, even if your own connection works
Its pixel-art sprite was traced from the famous T. rex skeleton "Sue" in Chicago

questions.explanation:
The team picked a dinosaur as a joke: without an internet connection, you're back in prehistoric times. The game came out in September 2014, and pterosaurs arrived as a second kind of obstacle in 2015.

The page appears when *your* browser can't reach the network, for example with Wi-Fi off. If Google's servers were down, you would see a different error, from a site that fails to respond.

The design team drew the sprite themselves. It has nothing to do with Sue or any other fossil.

Try it now: open `chrome://dino` in Chrome and press Space to jump.

questions.title: Where did the Go gopher first appear, years before the Go language existed?

options.text: On a T-shirt for a fundraiser at WFMU, a radio station in New Jersey
As a user's avatar in the Bell Labs email system
As the mascot of Plan 9, the operating system Go's creators worked on
In the logo of Google Code, Google's old project-hosting site

questions.explanation:
Around 1999, long before Go, the radio station WFMU asked illustrator Renée French to design a T-shirt for its annual fundraiser, and she drew a gopher. When Go launched as open source in 2009, French suggested adapting that gopher as the mascot.

Two of the wrong answers are close. The gopher's *second* appearance was as Bob Flandrena's avatar in the Bell Labs mail system. Plan 9's mascot is Glenda, a rabbit French also drew, which the Go blog calls a distant cousin of the gopher.

The gopher has no name. It is just the Go gopher.
questions.references: [The Go Blog: The Go Gopher (Rob Pike and Andrew Gerrand, 2014)](https://go.dev/blog/gopher)

images.alt: The Go gopher, drawn in black outline: a tall, round-bodied rodent with small ears, large round eyes, two big front teeth and stubby arms and feet.
images.caption: The Go gopher, by Renée French. CC BY 4.0, from [go.dev](https://go.dev/doc/gopher/).

questions.title: Which of these mascots has its creator dedicated to the public domain?

options.text: Ferris, Rust's unofficial crab mascot
The Go gopher
Duke, the Java mascot
Tux, the Linux penguin

questions.explanation:
Karen Rustad Tölva, who drew Ferris, released it under CC0. CC0 waives all copyright "to the extent possible under law", so you can copy, change and sell Ferris art without asking or giving credit.

The other three are free to use, with conditions:

- **Go gopher:** CC BY 4.0. You may do almost anything with it if you credit Renée French.
- **Duke:** the BSD licence, from Sun Microsystems. It allows commercial use and changes.
- **Tux:** Larry Ewing's own permission. You may use and modify it if you credit him and The GIMP when someone asks.

All four licences cover copyright only. CC0 says it does not waive trademark rights, and the others don't grant them. Copyright decides who may copy a drawing. Trademark decides who may use a name or mark to identify a product.

questions.title: Go's brand guidelines treat the gopher differently from the word "Go" and the Go logo. What is the difference?

options.text: The gopher is a drawing under a copyright licence, CC BY 4.0. The word and the logo are Google trademarks with usage rules
The gopher is a Google trademark, while the word "Go" and the logo are free for anyone to use
All three share the BSD licence that covers the Go source code
The gopher may be used only by official Go user groups and conferences

questions.explanation:
The guidelines say the word mark "Go" and the Go logo are Google trademarks, separate from the BSD licence on the source code. The gopher, by Renée French, is under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence.

These are two kinds of rights:

- **Copyright** protects a specific drawing. CC BY lets you copy and change the gopher, even to make a mascot for your user group, as long as you credit French.
- **Trademark** protects a name or mark that identifies a product. Anyone may use the word "Go" to talk about the language. Nobody may use it to name a different language or to suggest that Google endorses their product.

One project can have both. A free licence to draw the gopher gives you no right to use the Go trademark.
questions.references: [Go brand and trademark usage guidelines](https://go.dev/brand), [The Go Blog: The Go Gopher](https://go.dev/blog/gopher)

questions.title: In what year did Sun Microsystems release the Duke images under the BSD licence?
questions.description: Enter a four-digit year. Answers within one year are accepted.
questions.explanation:
On 13 November 2006, Sun announced that Duke would become "Free Graphics". It was the same announcement in which Sun said its Java SE and Java ME implementations would become free software, so the mascot and the platform were freed together.

Duke is older than Java. Joe Palrang created him as the "agent" character for the Green Project, the Sun research project that produced the Java language, and he became Java's mascot when Java was announced.

Sun's FAQ separated two kinds of rights. The BSD licence covered the *image files*. Sun claimed no rights in the *name* Duke and asked only that people not use him to disparage Java.
questions.references: [Duke Images project home (Project Kenai, archived)](https://web.archive.org/web/20150604165108/https://kenai.com/projects/duke/pages/Home), [Wikimedia Commons: Duke (Java mascot) waving](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Duke_%28Java_mascot%29_waving.svg)

questions.title: Which mascots are matched with their true origin?

options.text: Go gopher: a radio station fundraiser T-shirt
Octocat: stock clip art bought for an error page
Tux: a drawing made in the first public release of GIMP
Chrome dinosaur: the agent character of Sun's Green Project
Ferris: drawn by Renée French for the Go and Rust launches

questions.explanation:
Renée French drew the Go gopher for WFMU years before Go existed. The Octocat was Simon Oxley's "Octopuss", stock clip art that GitHub put on its error pages before buying exclusive rights. Larry Ewing drew Tux in GIMP 0.54 and let anyone use it with credit.

The two false matches swap details between mascots. The Green Project agent was Duke, who became Java's mascot. The Chrome dinosaur came from Google's Chrome UX team in 2014. Ferris was drawn by Karen Rustad Tölva. Renée French drew the gopher and Plan 9's Glenda, but not Ferris.

Few of these mascots were designed as logos. They started as clip art, a T-shirt or an error-page joke, and developers kept them because they liked them.
